claims.text: Premelting and melting in high-entropy-alloy nanoparticles are predominantly governed by chemically induced surface segregation.
Surface segregation enriches lower-melting-point elements at the nanoparticle surface.
Enrichment of lower-melting-point elements creates a surface layer with weaker cohesion.
A weakly cohesive segregated surface layer undergoes premelting at a lower temperature.
Mild annealing will promote surface segregation, whereas rapid quenching will suppress it.
Constituents with lower surface energy preferentially enrich the nanoparticle surface.
The resulting chemically altered surface film has reduced surface cohesive energy.
Individual elemental surface energies cause preferential segregation in multielement nanoparticles.
Weakened bonding in the segregated layer causes atomic mobility to begin earlier at the surface than in the core.
Early surface mobility lowers the effective melting temperature of the nanoparticle.
The segregation-mediated melting effect becomes stronger as particle size decreases because the surface-to-volume ratio increases.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit a lower premelting-onset temperature than rapidly quenched nanoparticles of the same composition and size.
Annealed nanoparticles will exhibit a lower overall melting temperature than rapidly quenched nanoparticles.
Rapidly quenched nanoparticles will retain a more uniform composition than annealed nanoparticles.
Nanoparticles with minimized surface segregation will melt closer to predictions from bulk HEA mixing rules.
The proposed trend should hold consistently for HEA nanoparticles smaller than 100 nm.
The segregation effect should become less pronounced in larger particles because bulk behavior becomes dominant.
Local chemical composition affects the stability of interfaces containing AlCoCrFeNi HEA material.
